title: The Convention

dialogue.text: The Assembly Hall has not been full like this since the inauguration. One hundred and twelve delegates. Four acts of the constitutional reform process. Everything you promised when you ran.
Theron is talking to Kolvar in the corridor. You can hear the tone from here. Not hostile. Something more careful than hostile.
And you believe that's workable.
I believe the drafting committee's proposal reflects the strongest available consensus.
Consensus among whom?
Among the delegates who engaged with the process.
And the ones who didn't engage. What do they think?
Theron sees you. His expression shifts — relief, or warning, or both.
Chancellor. Perhaps you can explain to Aldric that constitutional conventions require more than optimism.

monologue: Kolvar has been asking questions that aren't questions since the drafting committee formed. Every question is a probe — testing where the resistance is, who can be moved, who can't. He's not obstructing. He's mapping. The question is what he intends to do with the map.

choices.text: Delegate Kolvar — what specifically is your concern with the draft?
Aldric — where does the committee actually stand before we open the floor?
Vyktor — who's with us and who isn't?

dialogue.text: Article 7. The judicial independence provisions. The draft creates a Constitutional Court with appointment authority that bypasses the Assembly entirely. A chancellor appoints, a review panel confirms, and the Assembly has sixty days to object with a supermajority.
You're asking us to ratify a mechanism that concentrates judicial appointment power in the executive. We just came out of a government that concentrated everything in the executive.
The review panel is independent. The sixty-day window gives the Assembly meaningful oversight.
A supermajority threshold for a sixty-day window is not meaningful oversight. It's a procedural obstacle.

choices.text: What would you propose instead?
The supermajority protects judicial independence from Assembly politics. That's the point.
Aldric — I need twenty minutes with you before the session opens.

dialogue.text: Simple majority Assembly confirmation within ninety days. No supermajority. The Assembly can reject an appointment by majority vote. The chancellor nominates from a pre-approved shortlist developed jointly with the bar association.
That makes every judicial appointment a political vote. The court becomes responsive to whatever coalition controls the Assembly.
The court is already responsive to whoever controls the executive. We're debating which form of political influence is more visible.
That is a better argument than you expected.

choices.text: That's a fair point. Let's see if there's a middle position.
I hear the argument. I still believe executive appointment with independent review is the stronger model.

dialogue.text: The point is to protect judicial independence from Assembly politics. Yes. But the mechanism you've chosen protects it from Assembly politics by making it dependent on executive politics instead. That's a trade, not an improvement.
The executive is elected every five years and accountable to the electorate. Judicial independence from that accountability is the design goal.
We were all elected. Why is the chancellor's accountability more valuable than the Assembly's?

choices.text: It's a legitimate question. I want to discuss Article 7 in the drafting committee before we bring it to the floor.
Because a court that can be recalled by Assembly vote is not an independent court.

dialogue.text: Sixty-seven delegates in firm support. Nineteen in firm opposition. Twenty-six in what I would call thoughtful uncertainty — they have real questions and they're engaging with the process honestly.
The remaining delegates are waiting to see which way the room moves. They will vote with what appears to be winning.
We need sixty-seven votes to pass. We have sixty-seven. We have no margin.

choices.text: The twenty-six in thoughtful uncertainty — what are their actual questions?
What worries you most about today?

dialogue.text: Three clusters. Eight delegates from the rural constituencies are concerned about the regional autonomy provisions — they think the reform centralizes too much authority in Ashenmere. Nine delegates are focused on Article 7 — Kolvar is not alone in his objection. Nine more have economic questions — they want to know how constitutional reform interacts with the budget situation.
The economic question is the most solvable. The regional autonomy question requires real concessions. Article 7 may require reopening the committee.

choices.text: The regional autonomy concern — what would satisfy them?
Article 7 — what's the minimum change that brings Kolvar's group on board?
I've heard enough. Let's talk about how we open the session.

dialogue.text: Kolvar. Not because he's wrong — his Article 7 objection has merit. Because he's been talking to Vael's people. I have the letters.
He produces a folder. Places it on the table. Returns to his notes.

Someone is funding the opposition to Article 7 specifically. The legal scholars who've been publishing against the judicial provisions — three of them are associated with the Vael-Kross Foundation for Constitutional Studies. Which was established fourteen months ago. Two months before the reform process was announced.
Remove Kolvar from the drafting committee. Today. Before the afternoon session.
Theron says it without preamble. Without historical analogy. Just a clean, cold recommendation.

choices.text: Remove him. If he's coordinating with Vael this process is compromised.
Removing him without evidence we can make public makes us look authoritarian. Keep him and watch him.
I want to confront him directly. Let him know we know.

dialogue.text: Sixty-seven firm. That's the threshold. One delegate changes his mind and we're at a special session. Two and the reform fails its first vote.
Kolvar has been working the uncertain delegates for three weeks. I don't know what he's offering but some of them are listening.

I want to tell you something before we walk in there. One of the delegates — Mirova, from Sevagrad — came to my office yesterday. She said someone approached her with money. She didn't take it. She came to me.

choices.text: Who approached her? Did she get a name?
What do we do with that information?

dialogue.text: No name. An intermediary. The approach was about Article 7 specifically — she was offered twenty thousand Krone to vote against the judicial provisions. She said the intermediary knew details about the delegate vote count that should have been private.
Which means someone inside the process is sharing information with someone outside it.

choices.text: I want Danika Oberlin's office on this immediately.
We proceed and watch. I don't want this derailing the opening session.

dialogue.text: His faction has eleven delegates. Removing him from the committee doesn't remove their votes.
It removes his ability to shape the committee's output in the room where it's being shaped. That's the point.
His faction will call it political persecution. We need to have an answer to that.
The answer is that committee membership is contingent on acting in good faith with the process. Is there anything in those letters we can make public?
Not without exposing our source. But we don't need to explain. We can cite process irregularities.

choices.text: Do it. Process irregularities. Before the afternoon session.

dialogue.text: Watching him means he continues to operate. He knows we're at sixty-seven votes. If he moves three delegates before the final reading, the reform fails.
We could approach the delegates he's targeting. Preemptively.
That's also politics. The kind Kolvar is practicing. I'm noting that, not objecting to it.

choices.text: Approach the uncertain delegates before Kolvar gets to them.
Let the convention proceed on its merits. If the reform can't survive Kolvar, it needs strengthening.

dialogue.text: You find Kolvar in the corridor. Alone.
I know about the letters, Delegate.
A pause. He doesn't ask which letters.
Then you know that several distinguished legal scholars have serious concerns about Article 7. That's not coordination. That's a community of practice.
Funded by the Vael-Kross Foundation for Constitutional Studies.
Academic funding is public. I'm not responsible for where the scholars find their grants.
He meets your eyes. He is not nervous. He was expecting this conversation.

choices.text: I'm telling you I'm watching. If those delegates receive offers, I'll know where they came from.
What do you actually want, Kolvar? Not Vael. You.

dialogue.text: A Constitutional Court I can defend to my constituents. Sevagrad voted for this government but Sevagrad is also three hundred kilometers from Ashenmere. Article 7 as written means the court that rules on regional disputes is appointed by the government that created those disputes. My constituents are not wrong to notice that.
A pause.
Fix Article 7 and I'll bring six delegates with me. That's not a threat. That's arithmetic.

choices.text: What specific change to Article 7?
I'll take the arithmetic under advisement. We open the session as scheduled.

dialogue.text: The eight regional delegates want two things. A guaranteed minimum Assembly representation for provinces regardless of population changes — currently the reform ties seats to census data, which threatens Dravenhollow and Thornfeld as populations shift. And a regional veto on national infrastructure decisions that affect their territory.

The guaranteed minimum seats is manageable — it's three seats, it sets a precedent, but it's not destabilizing. The regional veto on infrastructure is not manageable. It would make the national railway plan impossible.

choices.text: Offer the guaranteed minimum seats. Hold firm on the infrastructure veto.
Give them both. The railway plan needs to go through proper consultation anyway.

dialogue.text: The minimum change that addresses the core objection: add Assembly confirmation by simple majority — not supermajority — within ninety days. The chancellor still nominates. The independent review panel still vets. But the Assembly gets a straight vote.
It weakens judicial independence marginally. It adds eight to twelve votes. It's a trade I'm willing to recommend.
Kolvar said six delegates. I believe him.

choices.text: Accept the compromise. Amend Article 7 before the floor vote.
Hold the original language. Sixty-seven votes is enough.

dialogue.text: If Danika opens an investigation, word will get out before the session ends. That changes the story from constitutional reform to corruption probe.
The corruption probe IS the story if someone is buying votes in my constitutional convention.
Yes. I'm not arguing against it. I'm making sure you know what you're choosing.

choices.text: Danika investigates. We proceed with the session. Let both stories run.
Hold the investigation until after the first vote. Then open it fully.

dialogue.text: We have three options. Ignore it and proceed — risky if more delegates were approached. Report it publicly and pause the convention pending investigation — clean but derails the reform timeline. Or use it privately — let Kolvar know we know, without making it public, and see if he recalculates.
The third option is the kind of thing I usually recommend and the kind of thing you usually ask me to justify.
Justify it.

The reform passes. Cleanly. No public scandal that becomes the story instead of the constitution. And Kolvar knows we're the kind of government that finds things out. That's useful information for him to have going forward.

choices.text: Do it your way, Vyktor.
I won't use private leverage against a delegate. Report it properly.

dialogue.text: I will vote against the draft as written. I will encourage my colleagues to do the same. This is not obstruction. This is the process working as intended.
The process working as intended produces sixty-seven votes and a constitution.
Or it produces sixty-four votes and a better constitution. We'll see which.

choices.text: We open the session. Let the floor decide.

dialogue.text: You pull Theron aside. Kolvar watches you go. He knows what a private conversation looks like.

I was going to tell you privately regardless. Kolvar has been meeting with representatives from the Vael-Kross Foundation. I have documentation. He's specifically focused on Article 7 — the judicial appointment provisions.
Someone is funding opposition to a court that would have jurisdiction over corporate conduct. That's not coincidence.

choices.text: Remove him from the drafting committee.
I'm going to talk to him directly.
We proceed and we watch. Don't tip our hand.

dialogue.text: One hundred and twelve delegates are taking their seats in the hall. The draft constitution is on every desk. Four months of committee work. Sixty-seven years since Veltria had a constitution worth the name.
We open in ten minutes, Chancellor. How do we go in?

final_convention_choice.monologue: Sixty-seven votes. No margin. Kolvar and his six. Mirova and the approach that was made to her. Theron's folder. The Vael-Kross Foundation for Constitutional Studies founded fourteen months ago. Everything connects to something and I have ten minutes to decide how much of that I'm prepared to act on before I walk into a room and open the convention that defines this government.

choices.text: Open the convention with the full draft as written. Take the vote on its merits. Sixty-seven should hold.

reactions.text: Then let's make sure every delegate understands what they're voting on before Kolvar gets to them.
He straightens his papers. His expression says he's already running contingency calculations.

choices.text: Open with the draft but signal willingness to amend Article 7 before the final reading. Keep Kolvar's faction in the process.

reactions.text: I'll draft amendment language tonight. If Kolvar acts in good faith, we have a stronger document.
Kolvar will take the concession and push for more. Be ready for that.

choices.text: Open with the draft plus the regional seat guarantee. Bring the eight rural delegates in before the vote.

reactions.text: Three guaranteed seats sets a precedent. I want that noted in the record.
Eight votes for three seats. That's a good trade.

choices.text: Before opening, announce that an approach was made to a delegate and that the matter is under investigation. Let that be the first act of the convention.

reactions.text: That delays everything by at least three weeks. You understand that.
It also means the constitution that eventually passes cannot be called corrupt. That has value.
He looks at Theron. Then at you. Then he nods.
